title: Caesar Calls His Mutinous Soldiers "Citizens"
text:
In 47 BC, during the civil war, Julius Caesar's veteran legions in Italy mutinied. Among them was the Tenth, his most trusted legion. They had served for years, they had not received the rewards they were promised, and they refused to sail for the next campaign in Africa. They marched on Rome, demanding their discharge and their money.

According to Suetonius and Appian, Caesar went out to meet them in person and asked what they wanted. They demanded to be discharged, expecting that he needed them too much to agree. Caesar replied at once that he discharged them. He promised that they would receive everything owed to them, after he had won the war with other soldiers and celebrated his triumph.

The decisive moment, both writers say, was the way he addressed them. Instead of calling them "soldiers" or "comrades", he called them "Quirites", the word for civilians.

The effect was immediate. The veterans shouted that they were his soldiers and begged him to take them back and to punish the ringleaders. Caesar relented, and the veterans followed him to Africa, where the Tenth fought at Thapsus.
lesson: People often value belonging more than their demands. Showing calmly that you can do without them may remind them what they would lose.
source: Suetonius, Life of the Deified Julius, chapter 70; Appian, Civil Wars, Book 2, chapters 92 to 94
